items.stem: Which term describes a group of people related by blood, marriage, civil partnership or adoption, often (but not always) living together?
items.answer: Family
items.markingKey: Family: a group of people related by blood, marriage, civil partnership or adoption, often (but not always) living together. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “lone-parent family”? Give one example.
items.answer: A family made up of one parent and their dependent children. Example: a divorced mother raising two children alone.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a family made up of one parent and their dependent children); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a divorced mother raising two children alone. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “extended family” and “household”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Extended family: a family that includes relatives beyond the nuclear family, such as grandparents, aunts or cousins (e.g. grandparents, parents and children living together). Household: one person living alone, or a group of people who live at the same address and share living facilities (e.g. four students sharing a flat).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In Hanoi, a widowed grandmother moves in with her son, his wife and their two children. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: there is no single family type; households are diverse and fluid, formed by choice and changing over the life course (Stacey).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Zara, who lives in Colombo, shares a flat with three friends; they cook together, share bills and spend holidays together. Explain how a personal life sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Personal life perspective: what counts as family should be defined by people themselves: friends, step-relatives and others who give support and meaning can be “family” (Smart, Weeks’s chosen families).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using non-participant observation to research the meaning of “family” to young adults living with friends.
items.answer: Strengths: it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts; the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively. Limitations: the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect); the researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the meaning of “family” to young adults living with friends but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “household of choice”?
items.answer: A household formed by people who choose to live together, often based on friendship rather than kinship.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a household formed by people who choose to live together, often based on friendship rather than kinship. [1]

items.stem: In Bogotá, a widowed grandmother moves in with her son, his wife and their two children. Explain how personal life and postmodernist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Personal life perspective: what counts as family should be defined by people themselves: friends, step-relatives and others who give support and meaning can be “family” (Smart, Weeks’s chosen families). Postmodernism: there is no single family type; households are diverse and fluid, formed by choice and changing over the life course (Stacey).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the learning of basic norms, values and language in early childhood, mainly in the family?
items.answer: Primary socialisation
items.markingKey: Primary socialisation: the learning of basic norms, values and language in early childhood, mainly in the family. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “dark side of the family”, and give one example.
items.answer: The harmful aspects of family life, such as abuse, violence and oppression. Example: domestic violence and child abuse.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the harmful aspects of family life, such as abuse, violence and oppression); 1 mark for a relevant example such as domestic violence and child abuse. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “unit of consumption” and “instrumental role”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Unit of consumption: the Marxist idea that families buy the goods produced by capitalism, generating profit (e.g. families buying new technology because of advertising). Instrumental role: Parsons’s term for the breadwinning role, which he assigned to men (e.g. a father working full-time to provide for the family).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Diego comes home exhausted from a stressful factory job and relaxes while his wife prepares dinner and listens to his complaints. Suggest how a liberal feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: family roles are becoming more equal through changes in law, attitudes and women’s employment, though inequality remains (Somerville).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Advertisements in Singapore encourage parents to buy the latest gadgets so that their children will “fit in” at school. Explain how a Marxist feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxist feminism: the family serves both capitalism and patriarchy: women’s unpaid labour reproduces the workforce and absorbs men’s frustration (Benston, Ansley).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Kenji comes home exhausted from a stressful factory job and relaxes while his wife prepares dinner and listens to his complaints. Compare how radical feminist and functionalist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: the family is a patriarchal institution in which men benefit from women’s unpaid domestic and emotional labour and domestic violence maintains male control (Delphy and Leonard). Functionalism: the family performs vital functions for society and its members, such as primary socialisation and the stabilisation of adult personalities; changes in family structure reflect the needs of the economy, as the isolated nuclear family fits industrial society (Parsons, Murdock).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying the experiences of women doing the triple shift.
items.answer: Strengths: response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of women doing the triple shift but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful case studies are for studying the impact of advertising on family spending.
items.answer: Strengths: they may use several methods, increasing validity; they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community. Limitations: a single case cannot show how widespread a pattern is; the researcher’s interpretation may be biased. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the impact of advertising on family spending but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “social mobility”? Give one example.
items.answer: Movement of people up or down the class structure. Example: a factory worker’s child becoming a doctor.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (movement of people up or down the class structure); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a factory worker’s child becoming a doctor. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “industrialisation” and “urbanisation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Industrialisation: the process by which an economy changes from being based mainly on agriculture to being based on factories and manufacturing (e.g. the growth of textile factories in nineteenth-century cities). Urbanisation: the growth in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities (e.g. rural families moving to cities to find factory work).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Isla lives 300 km from her parents in Bogotá but speaks to them daily by video call and they help pay for her children’s school fees. Suggest how a New Right sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: New Right: the traditional nuclear family with married parents and a male breadwinner is the best environment for raising children; the growth of lone-parent families and cohabitation threatens social order and creates welfare dependency (Murray).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Amara is planning a study of family relationships among migrants from rural areas to Karachi. Evaluate the use of longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; comparing the same people at different points avoids the problem of comparing different samples. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying family relationships among migrants from rural areas to Karachi but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “structural differentiation”.
items.answer: The process by which specialist institutions develop to take over functions once performed by the family.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the process by which specialist institutions develop to take over functions once performed by the family. [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research family relationships among migrants from rural areas to Cairo.
items.answer: Strengths: there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying family relationships among migrants from rural areas to Cairo but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “cereal packet family” and “family diversity”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Cereal packet family: the stereotypical image of the nuclear family (married parents, two children, male breadwinner) often presented in advertising (e.g. advertisements showing a smiling mother serving breakfast to a husband and two children). Family diversity: the existence of a wide variety of family types and household arrangements in a society (e.g. nuclear, lone-parent, same-sex and reconstituted families living in the same street).

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of covert participant observation for studying how people define who counts as “family”.
items.answer: Strengths: it can give access to closed or deviant groups who would refuse an overt researcher; because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided. Limitations: the researcher may be drawn into illegal or harmful activity and is at risk if discovered; note-taking is difficult, so data depends on memory and may be inaccurate. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how people define who counts as “family” but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “personal life perspective” and “pure relationship”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Personal life perspective: an approach that studies the relationships people themselves see as important, including non-kin and pets (e.g. a person who regards a close friend as “family”). Pure relationship: Giddens’s term for a relationship entered into for its own sake and lasting only as long as it satisfies both partners (e.g. a couple who stay together only while both are happy).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Samuel is planning a study of how children experience life in reconstituted families. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how children experience life in reconstituted families but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).

items.stem: Source A: “In a study in Kuala Lumpur, 300 couples completed time-use diaries for one week. Women in full-time work spent an average of 16 hours a week on housework and 10 hours on childcare; men in full-time work spent 8 hours and 6 hours. Women also reported more stress about “keeping the family happy”.” Use Source A and your own knowledge to answer the questions. (a) Using Source A, explain one strength of the method used for studying the division of labour in families. (b) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying the division of labour in families.
items.answer: (a) They are often cheap to obtain and produced without the researcher influencing them. (b) They are usually unrepresentative because only some people keep or publish them.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant strength; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2]

items.stem: Read Source A. “In a study in Seoul, 300 couples completed time-use diaries for one week. Women in full-time work spent an average of 16 hours a week on housework and 10 hours on childcare; men in full-time work spent 8 hours and 6 hours. Women also reported more stress about “keeping the family happy”.” (a) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that the family mainly benefits men.
items.answer: (a) 1. Women in full-time work spent more time on housework and childcare than men. 2. Women reported more stress about keeping the family happy (emotional work). (b) For: The source shows women doing more domestic and emotional labour even when in full-time work; radical feminists argue men benefit from this exploitation. Against: Functionalists argue the family benefits all members and society; liberal feminists note gradual change; diaries depend on accurate recording; 300 couples in one city may be unrepresentative. Also consider how far a single study using personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Official data for Madrid show where dependent children live, based on a sample of 400 children. Table: percentage of dependent children living | 1995 | 2025. With married parents | 73% | 58%. With cohabiting parents | 8% | 13%. With a lone parent | 19% | 29%. By how many percentage points did the figure for With cohabiting parents change between 1995 and 2025?
items.answer: +5 percentage points
items.markingKey: 13 − 8 = +5 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Official data for Hanoi show where dependent children live, based on a sample of 600 children. Table: percentage of dependent children living | 1995 | 2025. With married parents | 78% | 66%. With cohabiting parents | 8% | 13%. With a lone parent | 14% | 21%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for With a lone parent between 1995 and 2025. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that family diversity is increasing.
items.answer: (a) 21 − 14 = +7 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for With cohabiting parents, With a lone parent; the figure fell for With married parents; With married parents had the highest figure for 2025. Postmodernists see this as increasing family diversity and choice. Qualifications: Most children still live with two parents, often married; Chester argues diversity is exaggerated; cohabiting couples often marry later. The data also come from official statistics of 600 dependent children in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 14 and 21; 1 mark for +7 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Zara lives with her new partner, her two children from her first marriage and his daughter, who stays every other weekend. Explain how a personal life sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Personal life perspective: what counts as family should be defined by people themselves: friends, step-relatives and others who give support and meaning can be “family” (Smart, Weeks’s chosen families).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using laboratory experiments to research how children experience life in reconstituted families.
items.answer: Strengths: results are quantitative and easy to compare; the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified. Limitations: many social issues cannot be studied in a laboratory for ethical or practical reasons; it is impossible to control all the variables that affect human behaviour. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how children experience life in reconstituted families but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes Parsons’s term for the breadwinning role, which he assigned to men?
items.answer: Instrumental role
items.markingKey: Instrumental role: Parsons’s term for the breadwinning role, which he assigned to men. [1]

items.stem: State one criticism of the functionalist view of the family.
items.answer: It sees the family as harmonious and ignores conflict.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. it sees the family as harmonious and ignores conflict. [1]

items.stem: Explain Ansley’s argument that wives act as “takers of shit”, absorbing the frustration of husbands exploited at work, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Ansley argued the family soaks up men’s anger that might otherwise be directed against capitalism. Criticism: It portrays women as passive victims and ignores domestic violence by women or changing roles.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Marxist feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Sipho comes home exhausted from a stressful factory job and relaxes while his wife prepares dinner and listens to his complaints. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: the family performs vital functions for society and its members, such as primary socialisation and the stabilisation of adult personalities; changes in family structure reflect the needs of the economy, as the isolated nuclear family fits industrial society (Parsons, Murdock).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Madrid wants to research the impact of advertising on family spending. Explain one limitation of using covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: It involves deception and lack of informed consent, which breaks ethical guidelines.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the impact of advertising on family spending. [2]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which Marxists see the family as benefiting capitalism.
items.answer: Inheritance of private property (Engels); ideological functions – socialising children into hierarchy; unit of consumption; haven from exploitation (Zaretsky); reproduction of labour power.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Inheritance of private property (Engels); ideological functions – socialising children into hierarchy; unit of consumption; haven from exploitation (Zaretsky); reproduction of labour power. items.stem: Which term describes the growth in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities?
items.answer: Urbanisation
items.markingKey: Urbanisation: the growth in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “geographical mobility” and “structural differentiation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Geographical mobility: the movement of people from one area to another, often for work (e.g. a family relocating to a new city for a promotion). Structural differentiation: the process by which specialist institutions develop to take over functions once performed by the family (e.g. schools taking over education and hospitals taking over health care).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In Kathmandu, rapid growth of factories has led many young couples to leave their villages and live far from their parents. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: family life is now diverse and fluid; individuals choose from many family types and relationships, so there is no longer a single “normal” family (Stacey, Giddens).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In Istanbul, rapid growth of factories has led many young couples to leave their villages and live far from their parents. Explain how a New Right sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: New Right: the traditional nuclear family with married parents and a male breadwinner is the best environment for raising children; the growth of lone-parent families and cohabitation threatens social order and creates welfare dependency (Murray).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using non-participant observation to research family relationships among migrants from rural areas to Lisbon.
items.answer: Strengths: it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts; the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively. Limitations: the researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it; the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect). Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying family relationships among migrants from rural areas to Lisbon but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: State one reason for increasing family diversity.
items.answer: Migration bringing different cultural family patterns.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. migration bringing different cultural family patterns. [1]

items.stem: Explain two types of family diversity identified by the Rapoports.
items.answer: Organisational (differences in structure and roles, e.g. dual-earner or reconstituted); cultural (ethnic and religious differences); class (differences in resources and parenting); life-stage (families change over the life cycle); cohort (effects of the historical period).
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained type. [4]

items.stem: The table shows the family types in which 1000 dependent children in Kathmandu were living. Table: percentage of dependent children living | 1995 | 2025. With married parents | 73% | 58%. With cohabiting parents | 9% | 16%. With a lone parent | 18% | 26%. By how many percentage points did the figure for With cohabiting parents change between 1995 and 2025?
items.answer: +7 percentage points
items.markingKey: 16 − 9 = +7 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of non-participant observation for studying the experiences of children in lone-parent families.
items.answer: Strengths: children can be observed in classrooms or playgrounds without having to answer questions; it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts. Limitations: private behaviour in the home is rarely open to observation; the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect). Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of children in lone-parent families but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
